title: Sandpaper Grass
text: Did you know that humble grass helped reshape the teeth of ancient animals? It sounds soft.
nxt: But for a hungry herbivore, a mouthful of grass can feel like chewing sandpaper.

title: Forests Open Up
text: Over millions of years, the world grew cooler and drier. Dense forests broke apart into open woodlands.
nxt: In many places, a new kind of landscape spread across the continents: grassland.

title: Glass in the Blades
text: But grass hides a defense. Its tissues contain microscopic particles of silica, which is essentially glass.
nxt: Every blade is full of tiny, hard grains. Chewing grass is like grinding your teeth against fine sandpaper.

title: It Grows Back
text: And you cannot simply destroy it. Grass grows from the base, right near the soil.
nxt: If an animal bites off the top, the grass simply grows back. So grasslands are remarkably resilient, and the grazers keep chewing.

title: Worn Down
text: Animals with soft, short teeth faced a problem. Their enamel could grind down quickly, and a creature that cannot chew cannot eat.
nxt: Natural selection favored animals whose teeth could last.

title: Worn Down

title: Tall Teeth
text: Horses and antelopes evolved remarkably tall, high-crowned teeth. Hard enamel and softer cementum wear down at different speeds.
nxt: That uneven wear creates self-sharpening ridges, perfect for grinding grass.

title: Nowhere to Hide
text: Open grassland changed more than teeth. A predator can spot a grazing herd from miles away across the flat horizon.
nxt: So survival became a high-speed arms race.

title: Hooves
text: Herbivores lengthened their lower leg bones to stretch their running stride. They rose onto the tips of their toes, and those toes became hooves.
nxt: Their side toes shrank or fused into strong, springy levers.

title: Hunters Respond
text: Predators answered with longer legs, flexible spines, and stealthy hunting tactics.
nxt: Cats and dogs diversified, refining the art of the sudden, explosive chase.

title: Souvenirs of the Grass Age
text: So the next time you see a horse grazing in a field, look at its teeth and its hooves. Both are souvenirs from the age of grass.
